Authors: Guo QJ, Liu Q, Bossi P, Bonomo P, Colevas AD, Lee NY, Lu TZ, Lee V, Mehanna H, Ng WT, et al.
Journal: The Lancet. Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/S1470-2045(26)00347-5
Published: 2026-Nov-01
PMID: 42933448



Abstract:
Patients with de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma were historically deemed incurable and treated with palliative intent. Emergence of potent systemic therapy in combination with local treatment for both locoregional and metastatic diseases has enabled long-term survival in some patients. This international guideline was developed through consensus-building by 54 experts from 46 centres across 18 countries or regions and endorsed by 17 oncology organisations. 32 recommendations across seven clinical domains were formulated, including 29 strong (≥80% agreement [consensus] or high quality of evidence) and three conditional recommendations (67-79% agreement). We recommend that curative-intent treatment should be offered to medically fit patients with no more than three metastatic lesions in two or fewer organs at baseline or following response to systemic therapy; multimodality treatment (comprising immunochemotherapy, locoregional radiotherapy, metastasis-directed therapy, and maintenance therapy) is recommended. This guideline provides a practical framework for standardisation of clinical management of de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma and identification of key evidence gaps for future research.

Authors: Tao K, Lin Z, Zhang P, Chi P, Xiao Y, Hou Z, Xu X, Zhang A, Qiu X, Wu J, et al.
Journal: The Lancet. Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/S1470-2045(26)00446-8
Published: 2026-Nov-01
PMID: 42927765



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: To our knowledge, UNION is the first phase 3 trial to assess a neoadjuvant strategy incorporating radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy compared with standard care in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, which reported positive results for the primary endpoint (blinded independent review committee [BIRC]-assessed pathological complete response rate; 39·8% vs 15·3%). Here, we present a prespecified interim analysis of event-free survival. METHODS: This open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial was conducted at nine hospitals in China. Eligible patients were aged 18-75 years with untreated cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma (≤10 cm distance from the anal verge) and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1; stratified by clinical T stage and N stage), using permuted blocks, to receive neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy (25 Gy in five fractions) followed by two cycles of intravenous camrelizumab (200 mg on day 1) plus CAPOX (oral capecitabine 1000 mg/m2 twice daily on days 1-14 and intravenous oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 on day 1; experimental group) or long-course chemoradiotherapy (50·4 Gy in 28 fractions with concurrent oral capecitabine 825 mg/m2 twice daily) followed by two cycles of CAPOX (standard-of-care group). After surgery, both groups received six cycles of adjuvant CAPOX, and the experimental group additionally received adjuvant camrelizumab for up to 15 cycles. The primary endpoint was BIRC-assessed pathological complete response rate in the intention-to-treat population, which has been previously reported. Here, we performed a prespecified interim analysis of investigator-assessed event-free survival (one of the key secondary endpoints, defined as time from randomisation to radiographic progression precluding surgery, local recurrence or distant metastasis, or death) in the intention-to-treat population (all randomly assigned patients) with a boundary of a two-sided p values less than 0·0102. Safety was evaluated in all patients who received at least one dose of the study treatment according to the assigned regimen. The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04928807, and is active, but no longer recruiting. FINDINGS: Between July 23, 2021, and March 1, 2023, 231 patients (153 [66%] males and 78 [34%] females; 227 [98%] were Han Chinese, and four [2%] were other ethnicity Chinese) were randomly assigned to the experimental group (n=113) and standard-of-care group (n=118). As of Oct 1, 2025, the median follow-up duration was 36·7 months (IQR 32·6-39·9) in the experimental group and 34·7 months (31·1-39·1) in the standard-of-care group. The 3-year investigator-assessed event-free survival rate was 91·3% (95% CI 83·9-95·4) in the experimental group versus 77·4% (67·9-84·4) in the standard-of-care group (stratified hazard ratio 0·33 [0·15-0·71]; two-sided log-rank p=0·0029). During the entire treatment period, the most common grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events were decreased lymphocyte count (23 [20%] of 115 in the experimental group vs 31 [28%] of 112 in the standard-of-care group), decreased white blood cell count (13 [11%] vs 16 [14%]), decreased neutrophil count (13 [11%] vs 13 [12%]), and decreased platelet count (seven [6%] vs 15 [13%]). Treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 22 (19%) versus 15 (13%) patients, with the most common being decreased platelet count (one [1%] vs six [5%]), and radiation gastroenteritis (two [2%] vs four [4%]). Treatment-related deaths occurred in one patient in the experimental group (septic shock related to chemotherapy, but unrelated to camrelizumab) and none in the standard-of-care group. INTERPRETATION: In this interim analysis, short-course radiotherapy followed by camrelizumab and CAPOX significantly improved 3-year event-free survival in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, with a safety profile similar to long-course chemoradiotherapy followed by CAPOX. Comparison of this promising new treatment strategy with contemporary total neoadjuvant therapy strategies is warranted. FUNDING: Key Clinical Research Initiative Program of Union Hospital, National Key Technology Research and Development Programme of Hubei Province, and Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals. TRANSLATION: For the Chinese translation of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

Authors: Ramanathan A, Tilakaratne WM
Journal: Oral diseases | DOI: 10.1111/odi.70553
Published: 2026-Oct-27
PMID: 42935262



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Histological grading of oral epithelial dysplasia (OED) is the gold standard for predicting malignant transformation in potentially malignant disorders. However, traditional grading systems suffer from subjectivity and poor diagnostic reproducibility, complicating patient management. This narrative review evaluates the clinical utility of current and emerging OED grading systems. METHODS: We reviewed recent literature (2019-2026) comparing the traditional World Health Organization (WHO) classifications against binary grading, histopathological feature-specific models (two-point and six-point systems), diagnostic biomarkers, and clinical risk factors. RESULTS: The WHO system frequently demonstrates poor-to-fair interobserver agreement. Conversely, binary and six-point grading systems provide superior reproducibility. While these models effectively stratify malignant transformation risk, their clinical utility is limited by tissue sampling errors, such as "skip areas." Furthermore, immunohistochemical biomarkers (Keratin 13 and 17) show promise as diagnostic adjuncts to assist in identifying high-risk variants like differentiated dysplasia. CONCLUSION: While the WHO system remains the gold standard, its subjectivity complicates clinical decisions. Adopting objective binary and feature-specific models offers superior clinical utility for risk stratification. Clear numerical cutoffs alongside expanded morphological features and biomarkers may influence the accuracy of predicting malignant transformation, inform clinical decision-making regarding surgical versus conservative surveillance, and optimize patient management when integrated with clinicopathological findings.

Authors: Ketschau J, Grabenhorst A, Singer H, Kram H, Krautkremer N, Leopold C, Mohr J, Pippich K, Wolff KD, Ohayon C, et al.
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70528
Published: 2026-Oct-26
PMID: 42935021



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Contralateral nodal recurrence in lateralized floor-of-mouth squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains difficult to predict, and objective preoperative parameters to guide contralateral neck management in tumors without midline crossing are lacking. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 97 patients with lateral floor-of-mouth OSCC treated by surgical resection and neck dissection. Depth of invasion (DOI) was evaluated using endpoint-specific univariable Cox regression. Contralateral nodal disease was analyzed in patients without midline crossing (n = 68) using a composite endpoint of occult contralateral nodal metastasis and/or subsequent contralateral nodal recurrence. Tumor-to-midline distance was assessed on standardized multiplanar preoperative CT or MRI. RESULTS: DOI was associated with local recurrence (HR 1.322 per mm, 95% CI 1.131-1.545, p < 0.001) and ipsilateral regional recurrence (HR 1.199, 95% CI 1.052-1.367, p = 0.007), but not with contralateral recurrence (HR 1.030, 95% CI 0.834-1.272, p = 0.782). Among 68 patients without midline crossing, no occult contralateral metastases were identified in 19 clinically contralateral node-negative patients undergoing elective contralateral neck dissection. Four patients (5.9%) developed subsequent contralateral nodal recurrence. Midline distance was smaller in patients with an event (median 3.15 vs. 6.40 mm; p = 0.022; AUC 0.845). All four events occurred at < 5 mm (4/21 [19.0%] vs. 0/42 [0%]; Fisher p = 0.010). In time-to-event analysis, greater midline distance was associated with a lower hazard of contralateral recurrence (HR 0.622 per mm, 95% CI 0.395-0.981, p = 0.041). CONCLUSION: DOI showed an outcome-specific association with local and ipsilateral, but not contralateral, recurrence. In tumors without midline crossing, quantitative proximity to the midline was associated with subsequent contralateral nodal failure. The observed 5-mm threshold is exploratory and requires external validation before it can inform clinical decision-making.

item.title: #5 [0/100] Targeting the lactate receptor GPR81 suppresses tumor progression by disrupting glycolytic metabolism in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Okuda A, Funayama N, Hata K, Sugiyama M, Kobayashi-Ichiyama S, Wakamori K, Li LJ, Hirose K, Usami Y, Omi-Sugihara M, et al.

Authors: Okuda A, Funayama N, Hata K, Sugiyama M, Kobayashi-Ichiyama S, Wakamori K, Li LJ, Hirose K, Usami Y, Omi-Sugihara M, et al.
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108188
Published: 2026-Oct-26
PMID: 42933364



Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Cancer cells reprogram glucose metabolism toward aerobic glycolysis, a phenomenon known as the Warburg effect. This metabolic shift results in substantial lactate accumulation within the tumor microenvironment. Although lactate has been implicated in tumor aggressiveness, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Recent studies have identified lactate as an active signaling molecule that exerts its effects through G-protein-coupled receptor 81 (GPR81). The present study aimed to elucidate the clinical and functional significance of GPR81 in the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). MATERIALS AND METHODS: GPR81 expression was evaluated using human OSCC tissue specimens (n = 84). In vitro functional assays and xenograft studies were performed using GPR81-knockdown HSC-3 and SAS cell lines. The role of GPR81 in oral carcinogenesis was further examined using an immunocompetent 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4-NQO)-induced carcinogenesis model in Gpr81 knockout mice. RESULTS: GPR81 expression was significantly higher in OSCC specimens than in normal oral mucosa. GPR81 knockdown suppressed cell proliferation and tumor formation in OSCC models. In the 4-NQO-induced carcinogenesis model, the area of squamous cell carcinoma within the tongue was significantly reduced in Gpr81 knockout mice compared with wild-type controls. Mechanistically, GPR81 knockdown reduced ATP production and was associated with decreased expression of glycolytic genes including PFKL, PKM2 and LDHA. CONCLUSION: Through a multi-model approach, we identify GPR81 as an important regulator of oral carcinogenesis via glycolytic reprogramming. These findings suggest that targeting the lactate-GPR81 signaling axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for aggressive OSCC.

Authors: Habib MI, Sayeed MA, Islam M, Sarker MFR, Shakil SS, Hassan MM, Forwood JK, Ahad A, Islam A
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0361561
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42932356



Abstract:
Pigeons and quail contribute to poultry production, nutrition, and livelihoods in Bangladesh; however, their role in avian influenza virus (AIV) circulation remains poorly understood. These poultry species are widely reared and traded alongside chickens and ducks in household farms, commercial systems, and live bird markets, where inadequate biosecurity may create an overlooked ecological niche for AIV circulation, reassortment, and potential zoonotic spillover. Between November 2021 and April 2022, we conducted a cross-sectional study in Chattogram, Bangladesh, to estimate the prevalence and subtype-specific distribution of AIV and to identify factors associated with AIV positivity in pigeons and quail. A total of 300 birds (108 pigeons and 192 quail) were sampled from households, commercial farms, and live bird markets. Oropharyngeal and cloacal swabs were collected from each bird and tested for the AIV matrix gene using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, followed by subtype-specific detection of H5, H7, and H9. Data collected from bird owners and traders included bird demographic characteristics, bird source, and health status using a structured questionnaire. The overall prevalence of AIV was 14.3% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.6-18.8). Quail had a higher prevalence (18.2%, 95% CI: 13.0-24.4) than pigeons (7.4%, 95% CI: 3.3-14.1). Among detected subtypes, H9 was most prevalent (11.3%, 95% CI: 7.9-15.4), followed by hemagglutinin (HA)-untyped (2.7%, 95% CI: 1.2-5.1) and H5 (0.3%, 95% CI: 0.001-1.8), while H7 was not detected. Quail had higher odds of AIV positivity than pigeons (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 4.1, 95% CI: 1.8-10.6); clinically sick birds (aOR = 2.9, 95% CI: 1.4-6.2) and birds sampled from household farms (aOR = 2.8, 95% CI: 1.2-6.5) also had higher odds of AIV positivity. These findings indicate that pigeons and quails, which are understudied poultry species, may contribute to the maintenance and transmission of AIV within mixed poultry production and marketing systems in Bangladesh. Integrating these species into routine AIV surveillance is therefore necessary to strengthen early detection, inform control strategies, and reduce the risk of zoonotic spillover.

Authors: Hiratsuka D, Iki A, Kinoshita M, Doi Y, Kato O, Oshima K, Hiraoka T, Matsuo M, Ichinose M, Makabe T, et al.
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360619
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42932302



Abstract:
Infertility is a global health challenge, and impaired endometrial receptivity remains an important contributor to treatment failure. Endometrial dysbiosis, characterized by a low proportion of Lactobacillus in the endometrial microbiota, has been proposed as a potentially modifiable factor that may affect endometrial receptivity and fertility, and treatment with Lactobacillus-containing probiotics is emerging as a promising therapeutic approach. However, the optimal route of Lactobacillus supplementation remains unclear. We compared oral versus vaginal supplementation using the same Lactobacillus-containing formulation as an adjunct to standardized doxycycline/metronidazole therapy and continued oral lactoferrin in patients with baseline endometrial Lactobacillus <10%, based on paired microbiome profiling of endometrial samples (aspirated intrauterine fluid and endometrial tissue). In this single-center retrospective cohort study, thirty-two patients underwent paired endometrial microbiome testing before and after 30 days of supplementation (oral, n = 18; vaginal, n = 14). In the vaginal group, the median endometrial Lactobacillus proportion increased from 0.05% [0.00-0.20] to 99.15% [70.45-100.00] (p = 0.001), whereas in the oral group it increased from 0.00% [0.00-0.18] to 0.30% [0.03-66.33] (p = 0.005). The median change was greater with vaginal versus oral supplementation (+98.90% [70.45-99.80] vs + 0.25% [0.03-66.33], p < 0.001). Post-treatment Lactobacillus ≥80%, used as an exploratory marker of marked microbiota improvement, was observed in 9/14 patients (64%) in the vaginal group and 3/18 (17%) in the oral group (p = 0.010). Exploratory reproductive outcomes were limited by the small sample size and did not define a reliable clinical threshold. These findings suggest that, within this combined treatment regimen, vaginal Lactobacillus supplementation may provide a greater route-associated additional improvement in endometrial microbiota profiles than oral administration.

Authors: Intarasangkhanawin P, Orrapin S, Anuponganan W, Soonthornkes N, Mahawongkajit P
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0361495
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42932276



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Optimal mucosal visualization is essential for high-quality esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), particularly for the detection of subtle upper gastrointestinal lesions. Oral simethicone and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) are commonly used to improve mucosal cleanliness, whereas lidocaine ice popsicles provide effective topical pharyngeal anesthesia for unsedated EGD. We evaluated whether incorporating simethicone and NAC into a lidocaine ice popsicle could improve mucosal visibility while maintaining patient comfort. METHODS: This single-center, prospective, double-blind, randomized controlled trial enrolled 374 adults undergoing unsedated diagnostic EGD between December 2024 and June 2025. Participants were randomized (1:1) to receive either a lidocaine ice popsicle containing simethicone (100 mg) and NAC (600 mg) or a conventional lidocaine ice popsicle. The primary outcome was mucosal visibility assessed using a modified Total Visibility Score (TVS). Secondary outcomes included procedure time, water volume required for mucosal cleansing, additional simethicone use, endoscopist satisfaction, ease of esophageal instrumentation, gag reflex, patient satisfaction, discomfort, pain, and adverse events. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). RESULTS: All 374 randomized participants (187 per group) completed the study and were analyzed according to their assigned groups. Baseline characteristics were descriptively similar between groups. The intervention group had a significantly lower TVS than the control group (6.19 ± 0.51 vs. 10.39 ± 2.22; mean difference, -4.20; 95% CI, -4.53 to -3.88; P < 0.001), indicating better mucosal visibility. Exploratory segment-specific analyses showed lower visibility scores in all six gastrointestinal segments. The intervention group also had higher endoscopist satisfaction, shorter procedure time (10.87 ± 1.44 vs. 12.75 ± 0.96 min; P < 0.001), lower water requirements for mucosal cleansing, and less frequent use of additional diluted simethicone during EGD (12.8% vs. 96.8%; P < 0.001). Exploratory analyses showed statistically significant differences in gag reflex and pain scores, although the absolute differences were small. Patient satisfaction, discomfort, and ease of esophageal instrumentation did not differ significantly between groups. No adverse events were observed during the defined observation period. CONCLUSIONS: The combined formulation of simethicone and N-acetylcysteine incorporated into a lidocaine ice popsicle improved mucosal visibility compared with a lidocaine ice popsicle alone during unsedated EGD and was associated with improved procedural efficiency. This integrated formulation may provide a practical approach to pre-endoscopic preparation by combining topical anesthesia with mucosal cleansing. Further multicenter studies are warranted to confirm its effectiveness, generalizability, and safety with longer follow-up. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Thai Clinical Trials Registry TCTR20240606004.

Authors: Galli A, Tomasoni M, Salerno E, Di Santo D, Ferrari M, Missale F, Borsetto D, Mazzola F, Low TH, Gupta R, et al.
Journal: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery | DOI: 10.1007/s00405-026-10682-2
Published: 2026-Oct-26
PMID: 42931839



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Primary parotid malignancies are rare and heterogeneous. While comprehensive surgery with postoperative radiotherapy (PORT) is well established for high-grade and/or advanced-stage disease, the optimal management of lower grade, early-stage parotid carcinomas remains debatable due to their indolent behavior and low risk of nodal spread. METHODS: A multicenter retrospective analysis was conducted across ten tertiary referral centers. Patients with primary parotid carcinomas staged as pT1-T2 cN0/pNx and classified as low/intermediate-grade were included (2000-2020). Surgical procedures were categorized as partial (extracapsular dissection, partial superficial, superficial, selective deep lobe parotidectomy) or comprehensive. Time to recurrence (TTR), recurrence-free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS) were analyzed. RESULTS: A total of 129 patients met the inclusion criteria. Partial surgery was performed in 75.4% of cases, and PORT was administered in 37.8%. The 5-year TTR, RFS and OS was 96.6%, 91.7%, and 94.9%, respectively. Recurrence occurred in 3.9% of patients, with no regional failures and no disease-related deaths. PNI was linked to shorter TTR (HR 17.3, p = 0.002), whereas intermediate grade (HR 3.17, p = 0.035), older age (HR 1.03, p = 0.050), pT2 (HR 2.96, p = 0.045) and PNI (HR 4.68, p = 0.009) were associated with lower RFS. Only age was associated with reduced OS. The extent of surgery and PORT did not significantly influence TTR, RFS or OS. CONCLUSIONS: Low/intermediate-grade early-stage parotid carcinomas showed excellent oncologic outcomes in our cohort, in which we did not find an association between the extent of surgery performed and relapse or survival. The observed impact of PNI on TTR and RFS may support the use of PORT, according to the most recent ESMO-ASCO guidelines.

Authors: Cuddeford A, Mubaarak Z, Yussuf B, Ali S, Mavadia A, Gao C, Devabalan Y, Dhanani R, Zaidi AK, Iftikhar H
Journal: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery | DOI: 10.1007/s00405-026-10650-w
Published: 2026-Oct-26
PMID: 42931838



Abstract:
PURPOSE: This systematic review evaluates the relative safety and side-effect profiles of endotracheal tubes (ETs) and supraglottic airway devices (SGAs) for airway management in endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS). METHODS: A search of MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library was conducted in April 2025. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed for outcomes reported by three or more studies with comparable methodology; remaining outcomes were synthesised narratively. Primary outcomes were aspiration events, airway contamination and adverse post-operative symptoms (cough, sore throat, hoarseness, nausea and vomiting); secondary outcomes were operative time and estimated blood loss. Nine studies (714 patients, 1995-2024) were eligible. RESULTS: Aspiration was rare (one asymptomatic ET case). Pooled analysis demonstrated a significant reduction in airway contamination with SGA use (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.15-0.47, I²=0%). Device contamination was common in both (SGAs 0-86%, ETs 53-77%) but of limited clinical consequence. Pooled analysis also demonstrated a significant reduction in post-operative day 0 cough with SGA use (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.23-0.68, I²=0%), whereas day 0 sore throat showed no significant difference (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.24-1.74, I²=68.7%). Trends toward reduced hoarse voice, blood loss and operative time favoured SGAs but were not significant. CONCLUSION: The historical concern that SGAs offer inferior airway protection during ESS is not supported by current comparative evidence. In appropriately selected, low-aspiration-risk patients, SGAs represent a safe alternative to ETs. Given the heterogeneous evidence base, findings should assist rather than replace clinical judgment, with device selection guided by individual patient and procedural factors.
